title: Burst capacity sensitivity — annotated microtable (draft)
content:
Purpose / scope:
This is a working draft exploring how small bursts (2–30s) of traffic affect per-query latency and marginal token cost under different capacity accounting strategies. The goal is to produce a short, shareable microtable and a couple compact trends we can paste into a partner-facing one-pager.

Why this is different from the other bench notes:
- Focus on very short bursts (sub-1min) that are common in product experiments and release-day traffic. Most existing docs sweep longer horizons; we want the micro-penalty observed when prewarmed slots are scarce and tiling/amortization heuristics interact with reclaim timers.
- Emphasis on marginal cost for the bursters (who cause tail pressure) rather than system-average cost.
- Compact ASCII microtable and annotated bullets so PMs can read it in a slide.

Methodology (quick, reproducible):
- Workload: synthetic chat sessions (starter prompt ~60 tokens, average turn 80 tokens, typical session 3 turns).
- Baseline model: open-llm-sim-13B (quantized sim profile), single-region; GPU pool: 16-slot custom instance group (slot = 1x 80-token steady concurrency).
- Scenarios: steady QPS 50 (S), spike +200 QPS lasting 10s (B10), +500 QPS 30s (B30), +1000 QPS 15s (B15).
- Capacity policies tested: (A) aggressive-prewarm (keep 25% spare slots), (B) conservative-prewarm (5% spare), (C) on-demand-only (no spare prewarm, cold-start allowed), (D) hybrid-tiling (tiling + opportunistic prewarm).
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) per response, marginal token cost ($/1k tokens) observed for requests that arrived during burst window, and system-level cost delta for the hour.
- Notes: KV cache hit rates tracked separately; for these runs we simulate low locality (cache hit 15%) to amplify cold costs.

Microtable (annotated, read left-to-right):
Scenario | Policy | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | marginal $/1k tok (burst) | hour cost delta
S       | A      | 230     | 360     | 620     | 0.56                     | +3.6%
S       | B      | 240     | 430     | 810     | 0.52                     | +2.7%
B10     | A      | 260     | 420     | 750     | 0.61                     | +12%
B10     | B      | 440     | 920     | 2100    | 1.28                     | +24%
B10     | C      | 860     | 2200    | 5400    | 2.95                     | +38%
B10     | D      | 300     | 560     | 980     | 0.78                     | +16%
B30     | A      | 320     | 680     | 1400    | 0.95                     | +28%
B30     | B      | 720     | 1600    | 4100    | 1.96                     | +47%
B30     | C      | 1600    | 4200    | 11200   | 4.50                     | +86%
B30     | D      | 420     | 900     | 2100    | 1.45                     | +35%
B15     | D      | 360     | 760     | 1700    | 1.12                     | +30%

Quick annotations on the microtable (raw draft thoughts):
- Policy A (aggressive prewarm) buys p99 headroom at relatively modest steady cost; marginal $/1k tok remains low because we avoid cold-start heavy kernels. Good for latency-sensitive tiers.
- Policy B looks similar to A at steady state but collapses under even modest 10s spikes: p99 balloons because reclamation + slot churn amplifies kernel startup.
- Policy C (on-demand) shows why we cannot expose on-demand-only to higher-tier SLAs: marginal cost multiplicatively increases during bursts and tail latency is unacceptable.
- Policy D (hybrid-tiling) smooths the worst spikes but not as cheap as A in every case — tiling helps sustain throughput, but if the burst is highly concurrent and short, tiling setup overhead + partial prewarm misses create a mid-range penalty.

Representative ASCII trend (p99 vs burst QPS for three policies):
QPS  | A (agg-pre) | B (cons-pre) | C (on-demand) | D (hybrid)
50   | 620         | 810          | 5400          | 980
250  | 750         | 2100         | 11200         | 2100
550  | 1400        | 4100         | 11200+        | 2100

Sketch of marginal cost breakdown (for B10 on Policy C example):
- Kernel cold time: 40% of tokens (older sessions waiting)
- Excess GPU minutes billed due to spin-up: +22%
- Opportunistic queuing delay (bandwidth/time): manifests as p90+p99 jump
- Effective per-burst user-perceived cost multiplier ≈ 2.6x vs steady marginal cost

Operational takeaways (for product/ops):
- For release-day/campaign bursts of <30s, keep a small buffer of aggressive prewarm slots tied to feature flags. Cost of those slots over an hour is smaller than marginal cost blowouts when they fire.
- Consider a dynamic short-window auto-scale that separates "prewarm budget" from sustained autoscale to avoid oscillation with reclaim timers (timer 1: release warm, timer 2: sustained autoscale).
- Hybrid tiling is valuable for mid-duration bursts (15–90s) but needs tighter prewarm coupling to beat aggressive-prewarm for sub-15s spikes.

Open questions / things to validate next:
- Repeat with higher cache locality (hit rates 50–80%) — expected to shrink marginal cost gap.
- Try same sweep with multi-model routing (fallback to smaller model under tail pressure) to quantify quality vs cost trade.
- Test real traffic traces from PL feature X on 2028-06-21 to validate synthetic similarity.

Notes to self (copy for PM slide):
- One-sentence leaf: "Short sharp bursts can multiply marginal token cost quickly; a small pool of aggressive prewarm slots typically pays off for latency-sensitive tiers."
- Two bullets for ops: prewarm budget <-> feature flags; split short-window auto-scale from long-window autoscale.

References & links: GH:repo/issue#482 (bench harness), JIRA PLAT-1198 (auto-scale design), confluence draft (longer sims).

---
Draft level: rough; contains shorthand numbers from synthetic runs that still need a second pass and an explicit csv export. Prioritize: rerun B10/B30 for policies A/B/C with cache 50% and add 95% CI bands.

Unresolved: should we include an explicit fallback-cost curve for model-stitching? (ask Priya)
